verdict: Second read agrees with the first: clean. Literal search finds no Forbidden Language, no exclamation point, no hedge or connective filler, and one em-dash, which is the ESV's own in Philemon 16. Two of the five findings hold; three are dropped as over-editing. Nothing added.

keep.quote: The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, which required Americans to help return escaped slaves, points the opposite way.
keep.tell: Edit seam: a sentence left without its referent after a fact-check insertion (ambiguous framing)
keep.replacement: The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, which required Americans to help return escaped slaves, points the opposite way from Deuteronomy.

keep.quote: Some of the law meets a hard-hearted people where they are and restrains the damage they'll do
keep.tell: Stock church phrase ("meets people where they are") in the sentence carrying the essay's central theological claim; the one line that could run on any church's page
keep.replacement: Some of the law takes a hard-hearted people as they are and restrains the damage they'll do

dropped: "This isn't a modern sensibility pressed back onto an ancient text. It's the canon interpreting itself:" Dropped. It answers the skeptic's real next objection at the hinge of the section, the colon introduces a Scripture quotation and not a reveal, and the paragraph's opening sentence is a concession, not a second antithesis. The essay runs about one such turn per section, which is his voice.

"The church had both and looked past them for a very long time." Dropped. An accuracy worry, not a voice tell, and the subject here is the whole church across centuries, not the antebellum defenders the ledger's change 8 corrected. The proposed "read around" would repeat a phrase used two paragraphs earlier. Noted for James.
"Abolition had other engines." Dropped. A common idiom, used once and paid off three sentences later; changing it means rewriting three sentences to fix nothing a reader would hear.
for_james: The first reader's notes to you stand: the essay has no memory of yours in it (only you can supply one); "I pastor a Baptist church" states your denomination beside the Southern Baptist Convention's 1845 founding and 1995 repentance (your call); the slaveholder from The Monster in the Mirror is the book's composite figure in an essay where every other person is documented; your Substack profile and VOICE-JAMES-BELL.md disagree on length, paragraph size, the 'Monday morning' block and the screenshot line, and the essay follows VOICE-JAMES-BELL.md, which governs.

"The church had both and looked past them for a very long time." The fact check changed "skipped" to "explained away" for the slaveholders' preachers. This sentence is about the whole church over centuries, so it was left alone; if you want it to match, "explained them away" is the wording the sources support.

Closing Texts: the Philemon 16 line ends the quotation with a period where the ESV runs on with a dash ("as a beloved brother—especially to me"). It is a truncation, not a misquote, but the period sits inside the quotation marks.
Carried from the ledger: Noll's argument is checked against reviews and an interview, not his pages, and the Wilberforce diary entry stays a paraphrase.
